Breaking: Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

📅 28 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon.
  • It has been revealed that whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp.
  • Sources indicate that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 issue of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

It has been revealed that whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Sources indicate that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Sources indicate that absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

Industry observers note that IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

Hybrid cookware has already made a name for itself, and now the concept is making its way into bakeware. So what exactly is hybrid bakeware, and is it worth the kitchen upgrade? Let’s take a closer look.

Traditional bakeware usually features one primary material, such as aluminum, stainless steel or glass. Hybrid bakeware, on the other hand, takes a different approach by pairing multiple materials together. For example, durable stainless steel pairs with an easy-release ceramic nonstick coating. You get the best of both worlds in one pan.

Stainless steel and ceramic nonstick make a pretty dynamic duo in baking. Stainless steel delivers durability and provides a sturdy baking surface, while nonstick helps prevent baked goods from sticking to the pan.

HexClad brings these materials together in a distinctive way, and the magic is in the pattern. Industry observers note that hybrid bakeware can make everyday baking easier, from achieving consistent oven results to releasing delicate treats without damage. “Those everyday details matter to me when I’m deciding what deserves space in my kitchen,” explains D’Aniello.

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

Inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!).

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Sources indicate that cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

According to recent reports, pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Sources indicate that scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Sources indicate that just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Recent findings suggest that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Sources indicate that stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

It has been revealed that chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

In a recent development, I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

Chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. The pickles also do their job, adding just enough acidity and crunch to balance out the richness.

Industry observers note that my biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be said for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

Popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it debuted in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

It has been revealed that I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

It has been revealed that the mayo was another vital part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

Industry observers note that while Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

It has been revealed that chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

Chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.

  • Industry observers note that let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish!
  • Recent findings suggest that the key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Dirty rice has met its noodle match with our Louisiana-style dirty spaghetti.

Industry observers note that let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish! It’s a riff on Cajun-Creole dirty rice that transforms the original into an easy one-pot pasta.

Recent findings suggest that the key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme. And herein lies an vital cooking tip: When using store-bought seasoning blends like this one, give them a little taste first before adding anything to the pot. Different brands rely on different ratios of ingredients, and a tablespoon of one product could be much milder (or pack way more heat!) than a tablespoon of another. Your personal preferences matter, too. So whether you are sensitive to spice or like to pack on the heat, make sure you’re adding the proper amount of spice for your taste.

Industry observers note that dirty spaghetti is a riff on dirty rice, a classic Cajun-Creole side dish. Traditional dirty rice is made with chopped organ meats such as chicken livers or gizzards, which, along with the herbs and seasonings, color the white rice and earn it its “dirty” moniker. This dish, however, has a meaty base that’s made with ground beef and diced andouille sausage. Like the original, it also features the “holy trinity” of Cajun and Creole cooking: chopped onion, bell pepper and celery. A healthy dose of Cajun seasoning ensures each bite is packed with bold flavor.

Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven or large high-sided skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and cook it until it’s browned, four to six minutes, using a wooden spoon or spatula to break it into small crumbles.

Editor’s Tip: If you use a skillet, make sure it has a lid.

Add the chopped andouille sausage, onion, celery, red pepper and green pepper. Cook them until the vegetables are soft, about three to four minutes. Add the garlic and cook it until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Stir in the tomato paste and Cajun seasoning, and cook for one to two more minutes. Add 3 cups of broth and bring the mixture to a simmer.

Add the broken spaghetti to the pot, ensuring that the noodles are submerged in the liquid and separated as much as possible. Add more liquid if needed. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover the pot and simmer the pasta for six minutes.

Recent findings suggest that remove the lid and continue simmering until the spaghetti is al dente, stirring every two to three minutes. Add more broth as needed. Remove the pot from the heat, and season the pasta to taste with salt and pepper.

Leftover dirty spaghetti can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days.

The best way to reheat a pasta dish like this one is either in the oven or on the stovetop. To reheat leftover dirty spaghetti in the oven, transfer it to an oven-safe baking dish, cover it tightly with foil, and cook it in an oven preheated to 350 degrees for about 20 minutes or until it’s heated through. To reheat it on the stovetop, heat a saucepan over medium heat and add a drizzle of olive oil. Add the leftover pasta and sauce and saute them for about two to three minutes or until they’re hot.

Sources indicate that yes, you can freeze dirty spaghetti. After allowing it to cool completely, transfer leftovers to a freezer-safe container and store them in the freezer for up to three months. Allow the dirty spaghetti to thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating it.

The best pan for making this one-pot pasta dish is a Dutch oven or a large, high-walled skillet or pot with a tight-fitting lid.

First, be sure to give your Cajun seasoning a little taste first because seasoning blends like this one can vary widely in spiciness. Depending on how spicy your Cajun seasoning is, add more or less to taste. You could also make a homemade Cajun seasoning blend and customize the amount of cayenne pepper and chili powder to your personal taste. The andouille sausage also adds quite a bit of spice; for less heat, skip it entirely, or swap in sweet Italian sausage, breakfast sausage, chicken sausage or a milder smoked sausage like kielbasa.

Industry observers note that you’ll definitely want to pair this dirty spaghetti with crusty French bread, garlic bread or cornbread to sop up any extra sauce. Southern-inspired side dishes to consider include southern green beans, collard greens or black-eyed pea tomato salad. Or, complement the pasta dish’s spicy flavor with a fresh and crisp green salad.

Tech Report: The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat.
  • Sources indicate that gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake.
  • Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Sources indicate that gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

Sources indicate that there are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

In a recent development, “We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” notes Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef remarked.

Recent findings suggest that ursa began as a pop-up in El Centro, California, in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

It has been revealed that after helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee states.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

It has been revealed that “We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”.

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a fresh planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

It has been revealed that “We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee indicates of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

According to recent reports, ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

According to recent reports, “I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he notes. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”.

When the Days of Being Wild Come to an End

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This week, after reading up about the major differences between sea salt and rock salt, I found myself looking at a shot of my mates in an east London restaurant’s smoking area.
  • Industry observers note that it dawned on me that I’ve consciously uncoupled from chaos—an intense long-term relationship that, for many years, I considered an essential part of my personality.
  • I rather romanticized being a bit of a disaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week, after reading up about the major differences between sea salt and rock salt, I found myself looking at a shot of my mates in an east London restaurant’s smoking area. My friends looked happy—mildly drunk, joyous, their night still full of possibility—and I felt… hmmm… hard to say what I felt. Not jealous, not one bit, but also not relieved that I was home and dry. Maybe the word is content? Happy enough for them without longing for a sip from the same goblet.

Industry observers note that it dawned on me that I’ve consciously uncoupled from chaos—an intense long-term relationship that, for many years, I considered an essential part of my personality. Anyone who knew me in or around the summer of 2005—the thrifted grandad shirts, the Kate Moss for Topshop skinny jeans—knows I liked a bit of disorder, a grubbiness to the glamour. We dressed to go out, we went out, we laughed and toasted to nothing and smashed our empty glasses down. I would take sunglasses to pre-drinks because any night of the week could bring me the sun on the horizon. My party trick, without a doubt, was stamina. I have done walks of shame, drenched in thick glitter, at three in the afternoon. I wasn’t interested in looking after myself, or my surroundings, or anything that required sustained effort beyond the immediate gratification of the moment. I just needed somewhere to lie flat between merrymakings. I was rootless and selfish in only the way a person with almost zero real responsibilities, who’s still trying to find their way in the world, can be. Sleep was negotiable, meals were incidental. I wasn’t interested in wellness; I just needed a cigarette for the morning; and I don’t remember hydrating once in a decade—I was too busy getting on with things, preferably at speed.

I rather romanticized being a bit of a disaster. I think we all did back then. Blame Pete Doherty. There was something appealing about running on…erm…adrenaline, partying at capacity, being slightly behind on everything else. I mistook a lack of self-preservation for spontaneity and great swathes of disorganization for having a social life. I didn’t want to become one of those people who had everything Filofaxed; those people had missed the point of being alive.

According to recent reports, nowadays, weeknights find me with my trotters up in front of Red Dwarf, getting a little laundry done before bed. I’ve developed an unexpected appetite for maintenance: clean, high-thread-count sheets, say, or a handsomely stocked fridge. A house that doesn’t look as though a small twister has blown through, clothes that don’t scream French-robber-cum-mime. Doing a four-step skincare routine and going to sleep at a reasonable hour. Reading a physical book.

Industry observers note that I have become a man who likes things to be nice. I find myself taking pleasure in the small, unremarkable business of keeping things (and myself) in working order. There’s a time and place for the extraordinary, for the luxurious. But functioning, clean, and considered is eclipsing my more indulgent peccadillos.

I still like being out for dinner, and I still like bars where every drink is three-parts spirit, but I also like relieving the sitter by 11. I’m out with you; I just think, Wow, that was lovely; and then I leave. There’s no FOMO from the Uber, no twinge of the grass once being greener, of my body once being younger and more readily available for adventure. The cravings were gone, the mind-chatter silenced.

Recent findings suggest that I remain suspicious of people who seem to have turned being alive into an elaborate administrative exercise, a series of panic attacks about microplastics. My personality refuses to revolve around my cortisol levels or “sleep hygiene.” But I am beginning to understand that treating yourself like an afterthought isn’t particularly glamorous. Nor is being permanently exhausted. I don’t think I need to spend the rest of my life recovering from last night.

In a recent development, fatherhood accelerated this realization because fatherhood accelerates all realizations. There’s another person in my house who has very little interest in whether I’ve had enough sleep, whether I’ve eaten properly. She assumes—fairly reasonably?—the adults are taking care of things. Looking after myself, in turn, becomes less of a personal treat and more of a basic courtesy to the human I created. As a byproduct, I’ve discovered the pleasure of an ordinary day that doesn’t require damage control. I’m not dodging hangovers for the baby, per se, but I also don’t see the fun in keeping watch of a zig-zagging toddler while waiting for the Advil to kick in before your about-last-night apology tour. There’s something in a morning without regret, a house without a domestic backlog, an evening that doesn’t need to be wrung dry for every last drop of excitement.

Industry observers note that I’ve finally shed the conviction that being interesting requires a destructive streak. I haven’t become a different person, but I’ve redirected my night energy to a place of comfort. I’ve stopped treating my own life as something I can afford to neglect. Chaos and I are still on speaking terms, obviously; a toddler is the absolute essence of chaos. But I’ve decided one source of chaos—with a strict 7 p.m. bedtime—is enough for now. The party isn’t over, I’m just focused on the mornings after.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

Recent findings suggest that you can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

While you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a new lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

According to recent reports, in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in Latest York City.

It felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a upcoming role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

For me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

It has been revealed that “How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

According to recent reports, I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

In a recent development, as the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the looks I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

Recent findings suggest that the evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in Fresh York.

It has been revealed that in the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

It has been revealed that for dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

Recent findings suggest that as I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Julia Child's solution to a common turkey dilemma was equal parts culinary brilliance and holiday theater.

Julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach. She was a brilliant cook, a gifted teacher, and a woman who understood that a little butter could solve an astonishing number of problems. But perhaps her greatest talent was her willingness to question the rules, even when those rules involved one of America’s most beloved holiday traditions.

In a recent development, take Thanksgiving turkey. Most of us have spent our lives roasting the bird whole, partly because that’s how it’s always been done and partly because a beautifully browned turkey makes such a magnificent centerpiece on a holiday table. Julia, however, recognized a rather inconvenient flaw in this arrangement: A whole turkey is not well designed for even cooking.

According to recent reports, her solution was ingenious. She took the turkey apart, cooked its individual pieces, and then put the whole thing back together again for presentation. It was a triumph of culinary common sense, with just enough theatrical flair to make the whole thing unmistakably Julia.

Recent findings suggest that julia called her creation the “re-assembled roast turkey,” a technique she shared in her cookbook, The Way to Cook. Rather than wrestling an entire bird into the oven and hoping for the best, she removed the backbone, separated the leg and thigh portions, and roasted the breast on a bed of stuffing while the dark meat cooked in another pan.

Once everything was properly cooked, she arranged the pieces together on a serving platter, restoring the turkey to something resembling its original form. In her recipe, Julia cheerfully suggested that nobody would ever know the difference.

In a 2012 NPR Thanksgiving segment, Christopher Kimball, who had cooked alongside Julia, demonstrated the method with host Renee Montagne. The two had a wonderful time discussing the reconstructed bird, which they affectionately dubbed “Frankenturkey.” It wasn’t quite traditional, but that was rather the point. Julia had found a way to preserve the spectacle of a whole roasted turkey without actually having to cook one.

It has been revealed that the trouble with roasting a whole turkey is that its various parts have very different needs. The breast is lean and can become dry and stringy when overcooked, while the legs and thighs contain more fat and connective tissue, and generally benefit from cooking to a higher internal temperature. Getting everything just right at the same time is a challenge, even for experienced cooks.

Sources indicate that breaking down the turkey solves much of that problem. With the pieces separated, you can monitor their temperatures individually and remove them as they finish cooking. The dark meat has time to become tender without drying out the breast, and heat circulates more efficiently around the smaller pieces, reducing the overall roasting time.

Sources indicate that it’s a method we’ve championed at Taste of Home. Our guide to cooking a deconstructed turkey outlines the process of breaking down the bird, roasting the individual pieces and getting beautifully crisp skin. You can even ask your butcher to handle the disassembly if you’d rather not begin Thanksgiving morning with a pair of poultry shears.

And there’s another advantage Julia certainly appreciated: With the backbone removed, you’ve already got a head start on making a rich turkey stock for the gravy.

According to recent reports, of course, there’s no requirement that you follow Julia all the way through to the reconstruction. You can simply arrange the carved meat on a serving platter and bring it to the table. But I do love that Julia went to the trouble of putting her turkey back together. She understood that Thanksgiving dinner is as much about tradition and presentation as it is about good cooking, and she found a wonderfully clever way to have both.

Industry observers note that the result was better-tasting turkey that still got its moment of glory on the table. And if anyone could make taking a turkey apart and putting it back together seem like the most sensible thing in the world, it was Julia Child.

Tech Report: How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds.
  • Recent findings suggest that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop.
  • To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

Recent findings suggest that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

It has been revealed that if you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

According to recent reports, be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

Recent findings suggest that for a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Recent findings suggest that because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

In a recent development, for lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

Industry observers note that if you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Recent findings suggest that soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

Sources indicate that by hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

In a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

Secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

According to recent reports, this is probably a temperature problem. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Industry observers note that editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with latest reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Sources indicate that making a truly excellent bowl of mac and cheese shouldn't take an entire afternoon. Here's the one ingredient I rely on to get the creamiest cheese sauce every time.

I’ve made enough macaroni and cheese over the years to have developed some fairly strong opinions about it. Having two kids has given me plenty of opportunities to experiment, from throwing together the familiar blue box to baking versions that require several kinds of cheese and a considerable amount of attention. I appreciate a proper cheese sauce as much as anyone, but there are evenings when dirtying another saucepan to make a roux and standing over the stove with a whisk feels like an unreasonable amount of ceremony for a bowl of macaroni.

Sources indicate that which is why I’m particularly fond of a method that requires just three ingredients: pasta, grated cheese and evaporated milk. It produces an exceptionally creamy mac and cheese without butter, flour or any of the usual fuss, and it’s so simple that even boxed mac begins to look complicated.

Recent findings suggest that evaporated milk is regular milk that’s been heated until about 60% of its water is gone. The result is thicker and more concentrated than ordinary milk, with a richness that makes it especially useful for cheese sauces.

More importantly, those concentrated milk proteins help the cheese melt into a smooth, cohesive sauce. Ordinarily, adding cheese directly to hot liquid can be a temperamental business. The fat may separate, the proteins can tighten up, and the sauce can become grainy instead of silky. Evaporated milk helps keep everything together, doing much of the work that a traditional flour-and-butter roux would otherwise accomplish.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, one of the things I like most about this method is how little precision it demands. If you’re cooking a pound of macaroni, start with a 12-ounce can of evaporated milk and roughly 12 to 16 ounces of grated cheese. Sharp cheddar provides plenty of flavor, while Monterey Jack or fontina will give you a smooth melt. I generally prefer a combination, but there’s no reason to make a special trip to the store if you already have a perfectly good block of cheese in the refrigerator.

Sources indicate that I do recommend grating the cheese yourself, since the anti-caking ingredients in bagged shredded cheese can keep it from melting smoothly. Beyond that, there’s plenty of room for flexibility. There’s no need to measure everything down to the last ounce, which is part of what makes this method so wonderful.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Industry observers note that boil the pasta in generously salted water as you normally would, then strain it and return it to the pot, reserving about a cup of pasta water. Add the cheese and evaporated milk, warming them gently over low heat. Keep stirring until everything melts into a smooth sauce, adding splashes of pasta water as you go until it reaches your desired consistency.

Industry observers note that the same trick works beautifully in more elaborate recipes, whether you’re making a baked southern mac and cheese, a big pan of potluck mac and cheese or a comforting crockpot mac and cheese. All have their merits, but for an ordinary weeknight, I rather like knowing that one pot, three ingredients, and about as much time as it takes to boil pasta are all I need.

In a recent development, A handful of things are non-negotiable at Thanksgiving. You need turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and, of course, a slice of pie to round out your meal. And pumpkin pie is the undeniable star of the dessert table.

But sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

It primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That noted, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

Recent findings suggest that the pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

According to recent reports, once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez noted, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”.

Industry observers note that costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she remarked.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.

#134581. A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1871 w)

A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo.
  • On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge.
  • Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she said. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a big bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”.

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur remarked. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”.

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503.

The Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

Venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary latest guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592.

In a recent development, chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in New York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

It has been revealed that “You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

Calle Caonabo 35+1 809 584 9481.

Recent findings suggest that if, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

Calle Pablo Casals+1 809 562 6060.

In 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

It has been revealed that you’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Calle del Seminario #57+1 809 565 1621.

Hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

In a recent development, be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

Avenida Independencia 312+1 809 682 1433.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906.

In a recent development, on Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers quickly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580.

According to recent reports, across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

According to recent reports, pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

Avenida Cayetano Germosén+1 809 286 2141.

Recent findings suggest that at Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

Calle Ciriaco Ramirez 70+1 809 689 5544.

It has been revealed that the Colmado, Bur claims, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”.

Calle Luperón 52+1 849 460 5600.

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

Recent findings suggest that at night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”.

Avenida Lope de Vega 44+1 809 816 7200.

Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter stated, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

This Egg Wash Secret Makes the Prettiest Pie Crusts Every Time

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The secret to a beautifully golden Thanksgiving pie might be the simplest ingredient in your kitchen.
  • Thanksgiving pies have a way of bringing out the perfectionist in even the most relaxed bakers.
  • Sources indicate that an egg wash is supposed to give pastry a lovely golden color and delicate sheen, but getting it to cooperate isn’t always as simple as beating an egg and picking up a pastry brush.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

The secret to a beautifully golden Thanksgiving pie might be the simplest ingredient in your kitchen.

Thanksgiving pies have a way of bringing out the perfectionist in even the most relaxed bakers. Yet you might spend half an hour creating the perfect pie dough design, carefully crimping the edges or cutting little leaves from scraps of pastry, only to pull the finished pie from the oven and discover that your beautiful handiwork has browned unevenly. It’s a small disappointment in the grand scheme of things, but after all that effort, a little indignation is understandable.

Sources indicate that an egg wash is supposed to give pastry a lovely golden color and delicate sheen, but getting it to cooperate isn’t always as simple as beating an egg and picking up a pastry brush. Fortunately, there’s an easy trick that makes a noticeable difference, and it comes courtesy of a familiar face in the baking world: Great British Baking Show judge Paul Hollywood.

In a recent development, paul’s secret is simply to add a pinch of salt to the beaten egg. He lets it sit for about five minutes before brushing it onto pastry dough. In a BBC Food demonstration, Paul uses the technique to glaze scones, but it works just as well for giving pie crusts a beautiful, even finish.

In a recent development, beat an egg with a small pinch of salt until they’re well combined, then set the mixture aside for a few minutes. Give it another quick stir before brushing a thin, even layer over the pastry. The amount of salt won’t affect the flavor, and there’s no reason to make any other adjustments to your favorite pie recipe.

The difference is subtle but useful. Instead of clinging stubbornly to your pastry brush or collecting in the little crevices of a crimped edge, the egg wash spreads more easily.

Emiko Franzen For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever tried brushing a plain beaten egg onto pastry, you’ve probably noticed that it can be surprisingly thick and stringy. That’s because the proteins in the egg give it structure—a nuisance if you need to spread it evenly. Adding salt loosens those proteins, making the egg wash thinner and more fluid after a few minutes. It glides over the pastry more smoothly, leaving a light, even coating rather than stringy puddles.

According to recent reports, the egg itself is what gives pastry its golden color and glossy sheen. Salt doesn’t make the crust magically browner; it simply helps the egg wash do its job better. The result is a more consistent finish, particularly around the edges and decorative details where egg wash tends to collect.

It has been revealed that A pinch of salt won’t turn a lopsided pie into a masterpiece, but it can help a well-made crust look its best. And after we’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time weaving strips of pastry into a lattice for a Thanksgiving pie, I think we’re entitled to a little help with the finishing touches.

Give your Thanksgiving leftovers the club treatment by layering turkey and cranberry sauce with crisp bacon and lettuce. And don’t forget that middle slide of bread. We’re not animals, after all.

According to recent reports, need a break from heavy Thanksgiving fare but still have turkey to use up? Shred it, toss it with butter-bloomed spices, and tuck it into a pita with a bright, tangy slaw.

Recent findings suggest that in this play on a turkey club, the middle slice of bread gets swapped out for leftover stuffing fried in bacon fat. (We repeat: stuffing fried in bacon fat.).

Industry observers note that turkey and cranberry sauce already have a salty-sweet thing going on. Why not play that up by swapping plain bread for custardy French toast?

Though the recipe calls for cooked chicken, you guessed it—you can swap in leftover turkey seamlessly. The apple and fennel both provide lots of crunch and freshness.

Recent findings suggest that another chicken banger that works beautifully with leftover turkey. Boosted with red curry paste, tangy from Greek yogurt, this mixture is as good stuffed into lettuce cups as it is tucked between sliced bread.

This recipe sticks close to the classic turkey club, with one simple twist: a punchy, verdant herb mayo that comes together in seconds in the blender.

Roast turkey, tangy sauerkraut, melty Swiss cheese, and a tangy sauce? Heaven. Bonus points if the rye bread you use is studded with caraway seeds.

These 12 last-minute Thanksgiving desserts are the perfect way to level up your holiday spread in a pinch. Plus, they’re all super cute.

This year, why settle for the usual when you could elevate your holiday game with a turkey sculpture made entirely out of Rice Krispies treats? Imagine the look on your guests' faces when you unveil your masterpiece, glistening with cinnamon-sugar goodness.

Chocolate-Covered Strawberry Turkeys.

Recent findings suggest that when we need a quick dessert, a snack before the significant meal, or an activity that even the kids can try their hand at, these Oreo turkeys are a must-make. Charlie Brown Thanksgiving-Inspired Chocolate Bark.
