Scientists Discover Bizarre Deep-Sea Creature That Survives Without Most of Its Digestive System

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An unusual sea creature survives with much of its digestive system missing, thanks to a remarkable partnership with bacteria that could offer new clues about how life evolves.
  • Deep beneath the seafloor, where sunlight never reaches and oxygen is almost nonexistent, scientists have discovered an unusual relationship that may help explain how marine life survives in some of Earth’s most extreme environments.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery adds to a growing understanding of cold seep ecosystems, where life depends on chemical energy rather than sunlight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An unusual sea creature survives with much of its digestive system missing, thanks to a remarkable partnership with bacteria that could offer new clues about how life evolves.

Deep beneath the seafloor, where sunlight never reaches and oxygen is almost nonexistent, scientists have discovered an unusual relationship that may help explain how marine life survives in some of Earth’s most extreme environments. A deep-sea mollusk living in the South China Sea contains a previously unknown cellular structure packed with bacteria, offering new clues about how animals adapt to conditions that would be inhospitable to most other species.

According to recent reports, the discovery adds to a growing understanding of cold seep ecosystems, where life depends on chemical energy rather than sunlight. These environments contain abundant methane and hydrogen sulfide, which certain bacteria can use to support their metabolism. Animals such as deep-sea mussels, clams, and tubeworms have evolved close relationships with these microbes, providing them with shelter inside their cells in exchange for nutrients.

Until now, however, scientists had found no clear evidence that animals could develop specialized organelles dedicated to maintaining these bacterial partnerships.

The upcoming research centers on Chaetoderma shenloong, also known as the Divine Dragon Glistenworm. This unusual mollusk belongs to the aplacophoran class Caudofoveata and can grow to more than 150 millimeters (nearly 6 inches) long, far larger than most of its relatives. Its distinctive characteristics earned it recognition as one of the “Top-Ten Marine Species of 2024.”.

Recent findings suggest that researchers found that the animal spends much of its life buried tens of centimeters beneath the seafloor, in sediment rich in hydrogen sulfide and containing almost no oxygen. Understanding how it survives there led the team to examine an unexpected feature of its anatomy.

It has been revealed that using anatomical analysis, micro-computed tomography, and three-dimensional imaging, the scientists discovered that Chaetoderma shenloong has a digestive system unlike those of most mollusks. Its radula, a feeding structure commonly used by mollusks, is heavily reduced, while its midgut, hindgut, and anus have almost completely disappeared.

Instead, an extensive system of digestive glands occupies most of its body cavity. These glands contain enormous numbers of symbiotic bacteria that serve as the animal’s primary source of nutrients and energy.

Closer examination revealed something even more unusual inside the glands.

Industry observers note that the bacteria were concentrated within spherical structures measuring approximately 10 to 15 micrometers across. Each structure was enclosed by more than 20 layers of membrane and contained hundreds to thousands of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria. The researchers named this structure the dracosphera, Latin for “dragon ball,” because of its beadlike shape and surrounding layers.

A single host cell accommodated more than 1,600 bacterial symbionts on average. The dracosphera also lacked familiar cellular components, including host nuclei and lysosomes, distinguishing it from an ordinary cell or a typical digestive compartment.

This arrangement suggests that the mollusk may have developed a specialized structure for housing and maintaining its bacterial partners, potentially representing a previously unrecognized form of cooperation between animals and microorganisms.

The scientists then investigated how this relationship might function in an environment where oxygen is so scarce.

Genomic analyses of Chaetoderma shenloong and its symbiotic bacteria revealed that the microbes possess adaptations allowing them to maintain their metabolism with very little oxygen. The mollusk, meanwhile, lives deep in the sediment to obtain chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide that its bacterial partners can use.

Sources indicate that that creates a difficult balance. The animal and its microbes must obtain the chemicals needed to sustain their partnership while coping with the severe shortage of oxygen in the surrounding mud.

Recent findings suggest that one possibility is that the dracosphera’s many membrane layers help manage how oxygen moves through the animal’s body. The researchers propose that these layers could slow oxygen diffusion, allowing limited supplies to be directed preferentially toward the mollusk’s own cells while still supporting its bacterial partners.

For now, this explanation remains a hypothesis that requires further testing.

According to recent reports, the team also found evidence suggesting that the dracosphera participates in nutrient exchange. Digestion-related cellular structures and signs of enzyme activity were abundant around the regions containing symbiotic bacteria. These observations suggest that the mollusk may obtain essential nutrients it cannot produce itself by breaking down some of its bacterial partners.

Beyond explaining how one unusual animal survives, the findings may offer insight into a much older biological process.

Recent findings suggest that scientists believe that mitochondria, which occur in animal and plant cells, and chloroplasts, found in plant cells, originated through ancient relationships between microorganisms and their hosts. Over evolutionary time, these partnerships gave rise to structures that became essential components of complex cells.

It has been revealed that the dracosphera does not establish that a similar evolutionary transition is occurring in Chaetoderma shenloong. However, its distinctive organization provides researchers with another example of how intimately animals and bacteria can cooperate, potentially helping scientists investigate how specialized organelles and new cellular functions evolve.

The discovery could also have implications for understanding the broader deep-sea ecosystem.

Researchers identified traces of Chaetoderma shenloong at the mud volcano cold seep off Kyushu, Japan, and the Site F cold seep in the northern South China Sea. Together with previous records of large, closely related species in the Gulf of Mexico, these observations raise the possibility that animals with similar bacterial partnerships are more widely distributed across deep-sea cold seeps than currently recognized.

It has been revealed that such organisms may participate in the movement and transformation of methane, sulfur, and carbon within these ecosystems. Establishing their distribution and ecological contributions could help scientists better understand how life operates in parts of the ocean that remain poorly explored.

Reference: “A multilamellar organelle for chemosymbiosis in an aplacophoran mollusc adapted to anoxic cold seep sediment” by Yunlong Li, Chong Chen, Xu Liu, Menggong Li, Guoyong Yan, Haiyun Zhou, Hui Wang, Xiaoshan Zheng, Xing He, Shanshan Liu, Jian-Wen Qiu, Pei-Yuan Qian and Jin Sun, 30 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78965-0.

The work also received support from the National Key Research and Development Program of China, the Laoshan Laboratory, the Natural Science Foundation of Shandong Province, the Guangzhou Laboratory and research funds from the HKSAR Government, among other sources.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why late November 2026 is prime Uranus observing season.

The outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month. First, Saturn crossed this mark last month on October 4th, then Neptune followed suit on September 26th. Now, the planet Uranus makes the transition, crossing opposition next week.

Opposition occurs on November 25th. On âU.S. Thanksgiving-eve.â We say âoppositionâ for an outer planet, as a point at which it seems to rise âoppositeâ to the setting Sun as seen from our Earthly vantage point. Orbiting the Sun at a leisurely pace once every 84 years, Uranus has a synodic period of 370 days, meaning oppositions for the planet only slide forward about five days each year. This year sees Uranus reach opposition in the astronomical constellation of Taurus, between the Hyades and the Pleiades open star clusters.

Industry observers note that uranus at opposition for 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Shout out to the Full November Beaver Moon nearby on the same date as opposition 2026, fresh off of occulting the Pleiades for the Arctic on November 24th.

Recent findings suggest that uranus reached aphelion 20 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun in 2009, and is now inbound toward perihelion 18.3 AU distant in 2050. In 2033, Uranus will pass the point in Taurus where it was discovered by Sir William Herschel on March 13th, 1781, between the horns of the Bull very near the constellation's border with Gemini. Uranus made spurious appearances on star charts of the era at least 20 times prior to discovery.

Sources indicate that the discovery position of Uranus. Credit: Dave Dickinson/Starry Night.

Uranus reached its southernmost point in the sky in 2007, and crossed the celestial equator multiple times from 2011-2012. Uranus crosses the ecliptic plane northward in 2029. Uranus reaches its northernmost in 2032, and then begins the long trek southward. The Moon wonât resume occulting the planet Uranus again until a cycle starting on September 29th, 2029.

It has been revealed that the Moon occults the Pleiades on November 24th. Credit: Occult 4.2.

Observing +5.5 magnitude Uranus is as easy as sweeping the suspect field at low power, and looking for a blue-green âstarâ that obstinately refuses to snap into focus. To my eye, Uranus looks like a tiny planetary nebula or perhaps a distant fuzzy comet. In fact, thatâs exactly what Herschel thought heâd first discovered, back on that fortuitous night in 1781. He later correctly realized after following the new object for several nights that it was a distant, and therefore intrinsically large object far out in the solar system beyond Saturn, then thought to mark its outer boundary. All of this happened in his backyard garden in Bath, England. We can, however, be thankful that the name âGeorgeâ that Herschel proposed to honor his benefactor King George the III didnât stick (!).

One of Herschel's speculum metal mirrors and telescopes at the London Science Museum. Credit: Dave Dickinson.

Can you see Uranus with the naked eye? Topping +6th magnitude near opposition, itâs knocking on naked eye visibility from a good dark sky site. At the eyepiece, Uranus only highlights a 4â disk at around opposition, barely resolvable with a telescope and tough to tease out detail.

Industry observers note that A fine capture of Uranus from 2017. Credit: Szabolcs Nagy.

According to recent reports, uranus is tipped over 98 degrees (prograde) on its side, the result of some ancient encounter with another large body early in the solar systemâs history. At the moment, weâre staring nearly directly at the rotational (north?) pole/hemisphere of the planet, which will be pointed nearly directly towards us in late 2029.

Challenge: Catching the Uranian Moons.

Though Uranus has 29 known moons, only five are within potential reach of amateur telescopes, with +13.9 magnitude Titania being the brightest. Orbiting Uranus once every 8.7 days, Titania reaches a greatest elongation of 28â from Uranus. We once saw a sharp view of the moons observing through the Steward Observatoryâs Kuiper Telescope in the Santa Catalina Mountains outside of Tucson, Arizona. They were a surprisingly easy catch through the enormous 61â telescope.

It has been revealed that A fine capture of Uranus and its moons. Credit: Ralph Smyth.

A planetarium program such as Stellarium and Starry Night will show you the current orientation of the moons of Uranus, to help parse them out from any nearby background stars.

In a recent development, the orbits an orientations of the major Uranian moons. Credit: Starry Night.

The orbits of the moons are at the moment nearly perpendicular to our view in 2026, though theyâre edge-on and can transit Uranus as seen from our view once every 42 years. This last occurred on 2006-2009, and will happen again starting around 2048.

Hubble captures a shadow transit of Ariel in 2006. Credit: NASA/ESA/L. Sromovsky/University of Wisconsin.

Sources indicate that will we return to Uranus in the coming years? To date, only one mission has seen the planet close up: NASAâs Voyager 2, which flew past Uranus and its moons in 1986. Cassini-style orbiters have been proposed, though such a mission would be a lengthy affair, needing to first make the trip to the distant ice giant then slow down to enter orbit. As it stands, such a mission would be feasible for around the 2040s time frame.

JWST's view of Uranus and its rings. Credit: NASA/JWST.

Certainly, Uranus calls out for a dedicated mission. But you can explore the planet yourself tonight as it nears opposition for 2026.

Scientists Finally Solve the 1,700-Year-Old Mystery of 8,000 Dead Frogs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forests cleared for livestock in Roman Britain may have made young frogs more vulnerable to owls, revealing how human activity shaped wildlife nearly 1,700 years ago.
  • Industry observers note that finding 8,000 frog bones buried in a single ditch raised a strange question for archaeologists working along England’s A14 highway.
  • Sources indicate that nearly a decade later, researchers from Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) believe they have identified the culprits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forests cleared for livestock in Roman Britain may have made young frogs more vulnerable to owls, revealing how human activity shaped wildlife nearly 1,700 years ago.

Industry observers note that finding 8,000 frog bones buried in a single ditch raised a strange question for archaeologists working along England’s A14 highway. What had killed so many frogs, and why had their remains accumulated in one place? Evidence that the ditch filled within just one year made the discovery even more puzzling.

Sources indicate that nearly a decade later, researchers from Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) believe they have identified the culprits. The frogs were likely eaten by birds of prey, particularly short-eared owls and hen harriers, that took advantage of a landscape transformed by human activity during the Roman period.

Sources indicate that the bones were uncovered between 2016 and 2018 during the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme. After learning about the discovery through news reports, Dr. Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth University contacted Dr. Vicki Ewens, a senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, to investigate.

Clarkson compared damage on the ancient bones with patterns documented in previous studies and found evidence that the frogs had been eaten by birds of prey. Although this helped identify the likely predators, it did not fully explain how so many remains had collected in such a short time.

In a recent development, A closer examination of the frogs’ ages offered another clue. Using a pioneering method based on measuring their humeri, or upper arm bones, the researchers determined that most had died young, during the winter of their first year of life. Radiocarbon dating conducted by the University of Vienna placed the remains approximately 1,700 years ago, during the Roman period.

Sources indicate that at the time, Fen waters were retreating from the valley, creating favorable conditions for frogs to breed. This would have provided a plentiful food source for birds hunting in the area. Changes to the surrounding landscape may have made the young frogs even more vulnerable.

It has been revealed that short-eared owls typically hunt over grassland, yet the valley had been wooded during the Iron Age. To understand how the environment changed, researchers examined evidence from snails, pollen, and charcoal. Their findings showed that substantial areas of woodland had gradually been cleared to create grazing land for livestock.

Industry observers note that by the Roman period, large stretches of open ground had replaced much of the woodland. With fewer trees providing cover, frogs would have been more exposed to predators hunting across the grassland.

“We don’t often get an owl’s-eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” remarked Clarkson, who led the study.

Industry observers note that “The mystery of these frogs has been solved – a feast of frogs that were eaten and their bones left behind by a group of owls. These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world – what wild animals were getting up to in the past, and what life was like for them,” he added.

Recent findings suggest that the findings may also offer clues about how people used the valley during Roman times. Researchers suggest that communities may have visited the area seasonally to move livestock between grazing pastures. A less crowded landscape could have provided favorable conditions for hunting birds, although this connection remains a possible explanation rather than a confirmed finding.

What began as an unusual collection of animal remains has therefore helped researchers reconstruct both the changing environment and the activities of people who lived near the Roman Fens.

As Ewens concludes, “I had so many theories as to why such a large collection of frog bones was recovered from this small feature. It’s been great to collaborate with Paul to finally answer this question. This research indicates how even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “An Owl’s Eye View: Human–Animal Entanglement at the Roman Fen Edge” by Paul Clarkson, Vicki Ewens, Owain Scholma-Mason, Ellen Hambleton, Peter Andrews and Emma Jenkins, 17 October 2026, Environmental Archaeology. DOI: 10.1080/14614103.2026.2746302.

Sources indicate that national Highways funded the archaeological works for the A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme. Funding was provided by Bournemouth University post-graduate support grant for material retrieval, researcher travel, and radiocarbon dating.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness.
  • Recent findings suggest that luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns.
  • One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

Recent findings suggest that luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

This artist's illustration demonstrates the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141.

Dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

Dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

According to recent reports, âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â said Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â.

This image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and highlights the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi.

In a recent development, euclid introduced in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Big Bang.

Recent findings suggest that among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

Euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 fresh strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

"Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â mentioned Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 latest candidates.â.

Industry observers note that there's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row shows, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence.

Sources indicate that overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â said Srivastava.

Strong gravitational lensing is an notable tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

Recent findings suggest that finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly crucial in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Big Bang model of cosmology.

In a recent development, lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

It has been revealed that euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one significant grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each newly introduced data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

It has been revealed that but that won't be the end of cosmology. Latest questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy.".

Industry News: The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

📅 28 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.
  • The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.
  • This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Industry observers note that new to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he introduced Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Upcoming to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

In a recent development, adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“major plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

It has been revealed that eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

It has been revealed that this diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

In a recent development, ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the upcoming template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

These days, London has no shortage of excellent upcoming-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

Sources indicate that east Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

In a recent development, since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

In a recent development, this quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

In a recent development, the area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The fresh online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

According to recent reports, at the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

Industry observers note that there is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent New York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

In a recent development, clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

Sources indicate that while the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most notable British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

According to recent reports, joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Recent findings suggest that must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Industry observers note that shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

It has been revealed that bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

For my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy fresh surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Sources indicate that gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

According to recent reports, mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Sources indicate that together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

In a recent development, this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips indicates Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

In a recent development, the second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in upcoming-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

According to recent reports, fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

It has been revealed that must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Sources indicate that despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Industry News: Extra-Fluffy Cinnamon Rolls

📅 22 Dec 2022 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that at first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting.
  • Industry observers note that one is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough.
  • In a recent development, the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

Industry observers note that one is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

In a recent development, the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

In a recent development, yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

Recent findings suggest that this is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Recent findings suggest that yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

This recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Watch Zaynab perfect these cinnamon rolls.

Industry observers note that save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app.

Industry observers note that whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

Sources indicate that add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

According to recent reports, add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

While the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

Industry observers note that butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

Meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

1,000-Year-Old Welsh Legend May Have Revealed the Location of a Lost Roman Fortress

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A medieval Welsh legend may have preserved the location of a real Roman fort, raising the possibility that other ancient stories contain forgotten pieces of history.
  • The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.
  • The site is mentioned in Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig (The Dream of Macsen Wledig), a story about a Roman emperor who travels to Wales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A medieval Welsh legend may have preserved the location of a real Roman fort, raising the possibility that other ancient stories contain forgotten pieces of history.

The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.

The site is mentioned in Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig (The Dream of Macsen Wledig), a story about a Roman emperor who travels to Wales. Until now, the account of a camp in that location had largely been treated as a product of medieval imagination. But the archaeological discovery raises an intriguing question: can ancient stories preserve memories of places and events that have been lost to history?

According to recent reports, the Dream of Macsen Wledig is one of the 11 medieval Welsh-language tales traditionally grouped together as the Mabinogion. These tales blend history, folklore, magic, and legend, while some people see in them lost myths. Featuring kings, warriors, magicians, and supernatural beings, the stories offer a glimpse into how people in medieval Wales understood their past and the world around them.

The tales survive in two notable Welsh-language manuscripts: Llyfr Gwyn Rhydderch (the White Book of Rhydderch), compiled around the mid-14th century, and Llyfr Coch Hergest (the Red Book of Hergest), written toward the end of that century.

According to recent reports, but the stories themselves are older. They had been transmitted and copied since before King Edward I’s conquest of Wales in 1282, and perhaps as early as the 11th century.

Recent findings suggest that five of the tales feature Arthur, the legendary warrior whose tales spread throughout all of Europe. The Four Branches of the Mabinogi are a group of stories spanning the landscapes of Wales, Ireland and England, of this world and the supernatural otherworld. The remaining two, including The Dream of Macsen Wledig, reshape particular strands of early British history through native storytelling. All the tales offer imaginative accounts of power and political authority.

In The Dream of Macsen Wledig, a Roman emperor falls in love with a woman he sees in a dream. Determined to find her, he sends messengers to follow the route he has dreamed of. Their journey takes them across Europe and eventually to what is now Caernarfon, in northwest Wales.

Recent findings suggest that the emperor is called Macsen Wledig (Macsen the Leader). His character is a literary composite of a number of historical characters, most notably the Galician Magnus Maximus, a Roman general who became Emperor in the late 4th century. Born in a province that is now part of Spain and Portugal, Magnus Maximus seized power in Britain and went on to rule much of the western Roman Empire, including Gaul (roughly modern France and neighboring regions).

His legacy in Wales is particularly significant. In the popular Welsh song Yma o Hyd (Still Here), first released in 1983, the singer and former politician Dafydd Iwan invokes Magnus Maximus’s departure from Britain, supposedly leaving Wales behind as an entire nation.

The song draws on a powerful literary tradition – that the departure of Rome from Britain, just before the arrival of the English, saw the birth of Welsh identity.

But the medieval story is not a straightforward account of historical events. Like the song, it blends historical memory with imagination. Its importance lies not simply in whether every detail is factually accurate, but in what the story tells us about how Welsh people understood the past.

Recent findings suggest that the woman in Macsen’s dream is Elen Luyddog (Elen of the Hosts). She is also a composite character, associated with two figures named Helen or Helena – Helen of Caernarfon and Helena of Constantinople, mother of Constantine the Great. Both were 4th-century saints.

It has been revealed that in the story, Elen insists that Macsen travel to Wales to marry her. He agrees, and she becomes empress. Her father is appointed Viceroy of Britain, and together they begin building powerful fortresses. Elen asks Macsen to establish three towns: Caerllion (Caerleon), Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) and Caernarfon.

According to recent reports, she also asks him to build roads to link them. Sarn Elen (Elen’s Way) is still the name given to the main Roman road complex linking north and south Wales. The story offers a legendary explanation for features of the landscape that people could still see around them centuries later.

One passage in particular in the tale has taken on new significance following the archaeological discovery at Y Frenni Fawr hill in Pembrokeshire. Specifically, the moment in the tale which describes Macsen traveling from Carmarthen to the summit of the hill to hunt. There, he establishes a camp known as Cadair Facsen, or Macsen’s Chair.

According to recent reports, until recently, this reference was generally understood as part of the story’s imaginative landscape. But the discovery of a Roman timber fort on the hill, alongside coins dating from the period of the historical Magnus Maximus, offers a fascinating connection between the medieval account and the archaeological record.

It does not mean that every detail of the story is historically true, but it does suggest that the people who told and recorded the tale may have known about real places and features of the landscape that have since been forgotten. It also raises the possibility that other details in medieval Welsh stories could preserve valuable historical information.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery at Y Frenni Fawr reminds us that the past is not always neatly divided between history and legend. Medieval stories preserve important pieces of older knowledge, even when they have been reshaped over generations. By reading them along with archaeology, linguistics and an eye to the landscape itself, we may discover more about the people who once lived in Wales, the stories they told and how they understood their place in the world. By doing this, we understand more about the world we live in today.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid.
  • The lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying.
  • Industry observers note that to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

The lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

Industry observers note that to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

In the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

Recent findings suggest that but why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

Crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

But ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

Hera surveying asteroids with superhuman vision.
