💡 Key Takeaways
  • What remains in the brain after a psychedelic wears off could matter for future medicines, as rat scans revealed distinct activity patterns a week after three different drugs were given.
  • Psychedelic drugs are attracting growing interest as possible treatments for depression, anxiety, and addiction.
  • Researchers at the University of Southern Denmark compared three psychedelic drugs, LSD, psilocybin, and the synthetic compound 2C-B, using brain scans in rats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What remains in the brain after a psychedelic wears off could matter for future medicines, as rat scans revealed distinct activity patterns a week after three different drugs were given.

Psychedelic drugs are attracting growing interest as possible treatments for depression, anxiety, and addiction. Yet new research suggests that drugs often grouped together under the same label may affect the brain in very different ways, potentially influencing how scientists investigate their medical uses.

Researchers at the University of Southern Denmark compared three psychedelic drugs, LSD, psilocybin, and the synthetic compound 2C-B, using brain scans in rats. They examined changes in brain activity while the drugs were active and again one week later, after their immediate effects had worn off.

Unlike earlier studies that largely examined one psychedelic at a time, the direct comparison revealed distinct patterns for each drug. Only a few changes were shared across all three.

Industry observers note that “Psychedelic drugs are often discussed as if they work in the same way. But when we look at the brain, the differences are clear. Each drug appears to affect its own networks, and that is new knowledge,” states Mikael Palner, Associate Professor at the Department of Clinical Research at the University of Southern Denmark and senior author of the study.

While the drugs were active, LSD and 2C-B produced the greatest number of changes in brain activity. The researchers also identified different patterns one week later, suggesting that the effects of these substances may extend beyond their immediate action in the brain.

In a recent development, “What is interesting is that the differences do not only appear while the drugs are active. We can also see different traces in the brain afterwards. 2C-B mainly affected areas linked to reward, LSD affected areas linked to habits and motivation, while psilocybin stood out by primarily affecting areas involved in emotions,” says Frederik Gudmundsen, first author of the study.

Gudmundsen completed his PhD at the University of Southern Denmark and is now a postdoc at the Department of Clinical Medicine, Translational Neuropsychiatry Unit, Aarhus University.

In a recent development, these differences could help researchers investigate whether certain psychedelics are better suited to treating particular conditions. However, the brain activity patterns alone cannot establish which drug, if any, would be more effective for a specific disorder.

“If the drugs affect the brain differently, it is also possible that they may eventually prove better suited to different disorders. We do not know that yet, but our study provides a biological starting point for investigating it,” explains Palner.

Sources indicate that several psychedelic drugs are already being investigated in clinical trials for conditions including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and addiction. Understanding how individual substances affect different brain networks could eventually help scientists develop more targeted approaches to treatment.

For now, the findings remain limited to experiments in rats and do not show whether the drugs are effective in patients. Further research in humans will be needed to determine whether the same differences occur in the human brain and whether they can help guide future psychedelic treatments.

Reference: “Serotonergic psychedelics induce distinct patterns of metabolic activity and covariance within biologically informed rat brain networks” by Frederik Gudmundsen, Julia Czurylo, Daniel R. Rijsketic, Camilla Trang Vo, Janika Fortunato, Naja S. Jessen, Sophie Woodruff, Christina Baun, Matthias M. Herth, Vladimir Shalgunov, Boris D. Heifets, Patrick M. Fisher and Mikael Palner, 3 August 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75890-0.

The study was supported by the Independent Research Fund Denmark, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Lundbeck Foundation, Neuroscience Academy Denmark and the US National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Disclosure: The authors have also disclosed relevant potential conflicts of interest. Mikael Palner holds shares in Compass Pathways and AtaiBeckley. He has previously been involved in research collaborations with Compass Pathways, A7imuth, TetraKit, Arla, Cymap and Bright Minds Bio and is an adviser to BrandarisTx. None of these companies or relationships had any influence on the study.

  • In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

Industry observers note that now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Massive Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

It has been revealed that first, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Significant Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Peking University have developed a fluorescent dye that can distinguish at least 14 membrane-bound structures in living cells using subtle differences in their chemical environments.

Sources indicate that watching the inner workings of living cells has long been difficult because most fluorescent dyes highlight only one cellular structure at a time. Now, researchers at Peking University have developed a dye called JONR that can distinguish at least 14 different structures using a single stain.

The dye changes color depending on the chemical environment surrounding it, allowing scientists to identify cellular structures without labeling each one separately. In laboratory tests, JONR identified organelles with three times the accuracy of Nile red, a fluorescent dye that has been used for more than a century.

Industry observers note that JONR is based on Nile red, which glows differently depending on its surroundings. It produces greener light in oily environments and redder light in more polar ones. However, Nile red’s limited color changes make it difficult to tell similar cell membranes apart.

By modifying the dye’s molecular structure, the researchers increased its sensitivity to subtle differences between membranes. JONR also produces very little light in water, reducing unwanted background signals and making cellular structures easier to observe.

Using JONR, scientists were able to track interactions between structures inside living cells. They observed moving compartments called late endosomes pulling thin tubes of the endoplasmic reticulum, a network involved in processing proteins and other cellular activities.

In a recent development, the dye also revealed differences in how tightly molecules are packed within membranes. With specialized microscopy, researchers could examine both membrane composition and molecular organization using the same stain.

According to recent reports, experiments involving nerve cells showed that JONR could detect how molecules are arranged along nerve fibers. Additional tests in migrating cells revealed differences between the membranes of structures involved in cell movement.

The dye revealed no significant toxicity in cultured cells, but the research has not yet demonstrated its performance in living animals or humans. Some measurements also require specialized microscopes.

Although further testing is needed, JONR could allow researchers to study several cellular structures and their interactions without relying on multiple fluorescent dyes.

Reference: “Far-red-emitting Nile red with boosted solvatochromism enables multidimensional imaging of membrane heterogeneity and dynamics” by Mingqiao Liu, Yunzhe Fu, Xiaopeng Li, Haolin Zhang, Yumiao Ma, Meiqi Li, Chunyan Shan, Hongxi Zheng, Xiaoyi Lu, Yan Zhang, Li Yu, Peng Xi and Zhixing Chen, 23 February 2026, The Innovation. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered that twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets creates a hidden grid of atomic defects that alters how electrical charges are distributed.
  • Twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets together has allowed scientists to create a hidden grid of atomic defects that influences how electrical charges are arranged.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery, led by researchers at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and published in Nature, demonstrates how the angle between two bonded crystals can control the spacing of defects at their interface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered that twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets creates a hidden grid of atomic defects that alters how electrical charges are distributed.

Twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets together has allowed scientists to create a hidden grid of atomic defects that influences how electrical charges are arranged. The grid forms where the crystals meet, producing tiny patterns of electrical polarization that could eventually help researchers develop newly introduced electronic technologies.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery, led by researchers at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and published in Nature, demonstrates how the angle between two bonded crystals can control the spacing of defects at their interface. Although practical applications remain uncertain, the technique offers a way to engineer electrical structures at the nanoscale.

Industry observers note that the researchers worked with strontium titanate (SrTiO3), a chemically stable oxide widely studied for its electronic properties. They fabricated crystal sheets just 10 nanometers (about 0.0000004 inches) thick and assembled them with a controlled twist.

The underlying principle resembles a moiré pattern, which appears when two regular grids overlap at slightly different angles. However, strong bonding between the crystal sheets caused their atoms to rearrange at the interface. The remaining mismatch became concentrated along narrow regions of crystal distortion called dislocations, forming a repeating square grid.

Recent findings suggest that “We have spent years learning how to make high-quality sheets, put them together in the right position, bond them and twist them. Once you can do all of that, you can start looking at what happens where these two sheets meet,” indicates Professor Nini Pryds of DTU.

“So, the bonding is essential to understanding what happens between the layers.”.

The grid was first predicted by William Sandholt, then a Ph.D. student at DTU, using machine learning simulations to calculate how atoms would rearrange as the crystals bonded and twisted. His results identified a network of dislocations that the researchers subsequently searched for experimentally.

Early electron microscope images revealed what appeared to be an ordinary moiré pattern, with no obvious sign of the predicted defects. One difficulty was that the microscope’s electron beam passed through material on both sides of the buried interface, making its atomic structure difficult to isolate.

Recent findings suggest that “The electron beam goes through about ten nanometers of material, reaches the interface, and then goes through another ten nanometers. So, the image is influenced by the material on both sides of what we want to see,” explains John Mangeri, a postdoc at DTU and joint first author of the study.

To overcome this problem, the team simulated how electrons traveled through the samples and examined thin cross sections cut in different directions. Electron microscopy performed with collaborators at the University of Antwerp in Belgium and the SuperSTEM Laboratory in the UK ultimately confirmed the predicted grid.

Industry observers note that “Right where the sheets met, we could see the repeating pattern, and it agreed almost perfectly with the theory. That was amazing.”.

Pryds emphasizes that the theoretical predictions were essential to the discovery.

Industry observers note that “We would never have discovered the dislocations if the calculations had not predicted their existence. The finding highlights the power of combining theory and experiment, bringing together researchers who synthesized the ultrathin sheets, assembled them with a controlled twist, simulated their behavior, and examined the resulting material.”.

Sources indicate that further simulations highlighted that the atomic distortions surrounding the dislocations could slightly separate positive and negative electrical charges. This separation, known as polarization, formed swirling patterns around the grid. Additional microscopy, interpreted alongside the simulations, supported the connection between the atomic distortions and these electrical structures.

The spacing of the grid also depends on the angle between the crystal sheets, providing a means of adjusting the size of the resulting patterns.

It has been revealed that “Changing the twist angle changes the spacing between the dislocations. So now, we have a way to control how small the structure becomes,” says joint first author William Sandholt.

“These dislocations could be used for memory applications, for example, and the grid could be tuned through the twist angle.”.

It has been revealed that electrical polarization plays a role in technologies such as memory devices and energy storage systems, making these structures potential candidates for future research. The team prepares to investigate whether the same approach can produce useful electrical behavior in strontium titanate or other oxides.

Reference: “Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites” by W. Sandholt, N. Gauquelin, J. Mangeri, A. Annys, J. M. Hansen, A. R. Insinga, E. Dollekamp, N. Vitaliti, G. Panchal, T. Chennit, A. De Backer, D. Kepaptsoglou, R. Mandal, D. R. Rodrigues, S. Van Aert, H. Nguyen, K. I. Wurster, A. Bhowmik, I. E. Castelli, S. B. Simonsen, T. S. Jespersen, Q. M. Ramasse, R. D. James, B. Jalan, J. Verbeeck, J. M. G. Lastra and N. Pryds, 18 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11330-9.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., noted on Monday evening.

It has been revealed that asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

Industry observers note that “Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Recent findings suggest that johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

In a recent development, also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he mentioned, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

Sources indicate that in the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

According to recent reports, but Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, stated she has seen such requests rolled out in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that and several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the looks and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott remarked. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

Recent findings suggest that an online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick noted in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly noted Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday remarked the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” stated Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

It has been revealed that cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.

#134448. American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3437 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes.
  • In a recent development, “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes. Lindsey, who until early 2025 managed the federal government’s climate.gov website, had just begun to think her job might be safe during the second Trump administration.

In a recent development, “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years. “Every time you would hear the rumor and then it wouldn’t happen, you would think … maybe this is all just talk.”.

But at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer “fit the Agency’s current needs.” In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.

The Lindsey sisters decided to fight back. Along with another terminated NOAA employee, they split a $65,000 grant from the nonprofit Surge Climate Talent and debuted a crowdfunding campaign to rebuild and enhancement climate.gov. The site, now called climate.us, notched one million views in its first month.

Industry observers note that but as proud as they are of their work, the project is a patch, not a fix. Rebecca Lindsey predicts it would take at least seven employees and $1.8 million annually to resume 80 percent of the old site’s work. “Climate.gov was more than just a website; it was a climate literacy program,” she states. To rescue the full mission, they still have a long way to go.

In a recent development, courtesy of M. Lindsey and R. Lindsey.

In a recent development, the Lindsey sisters are far from the only tale of makeshift resilience. Over the last year, untold numbers of U.S. scientists and their supporters have rebuilt data dashboards, formed recommendation groups for childhood vaccines and screenings, and doled out research funds for hundreds of stranded early-career scientists. They’ve reconstituted committees to advise space missions, rehomed key reports on climate and Arctic science, and even turned to social media to spread public health alerts in the wake of a massive realignment of the federal science enterprise.

“I don’t think anyone could have foreseen the amount of destruction and deliberate breaking down of norms and infrastructure” over the last two years, says Christina Madison, a clinical pharmacist and public health communicator known on social media as The Public Health Pharmacist.

According to recent reports, since January 2025, the second Trump administration has frozen or rescinded billions of dollars in research funding on topics from climate change to vaccine hesitancy and is trying to redirect it — often without congressional approval — to administration priorities such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. During deliberations for the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, the White House proposed slashing future science funding by one-third.

“When this was first starting, it really, truly felt like an alternate universe,” notes Sean O’Leary, a pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “The science was always what drove the decision making, and now we’re at a place where it’s not.”.

It has been revealed that in 2025 alone, the federal government shed some 20 percentof its science workforce. And in May 2026, the Office of Management and Budget proposed a sweeping set of rules to expand the authority of federal political appointees in selecting science grants.

Approximate proportion of the scientific workforce who left federal service in 2025.

In a recent development, yet some researchers see the destruction as an opportunity to rebuild their corners of U.S. science — or even reimagine it, says Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “If there’s any good that can come out of what has been a horrible situation, it’s that it’s given us time and provided a pause to think through clearly: Is this the way we want to continue?”.

University of Ottawa ecologist Julien Martin spent a decade building a respected lab that probed how social behaviors affect the evolution of bushy-tailed, cat-sized rodents called marmots. So when the National Science Foundation began its sweeping grant cuts, Martin found himself doing something unexpected: uploading cute marmot videos to OnlyFans, an online video subscription platform better known for hosting pornography.

Industry observers note that the effort, called OnlyMarms, netted $6,000 — a mere drop in the funding bucket. But the project went viral, leading outside supporters to launch a cryptocurrency token that earned the lab an additional $150,000. And direct donations, including an anonymous $300,000 gift, gave the lab enough to fund one Ph.D. student’s entire degree.

Recent findings suggest that “When you see that so much money could be obtained by doing essentially nothing about science, it’s quite shocking,” Martin notes. He welcomes the support, but having to spend so much time on non-research tasks has also felt demeaning. “Sometimes, you have to question: Is the science funding broken? Are we just competing for pennies?”.

In a recent development, in 2025, the National Institutes of Health and the NSF canceled or suspended more than 7,800 existing grants, totaling billions of dollars. (Some 5,200 grants were later reinstated.) Each agency issued roughly a quarter fewer grants in 2025 than their previous 10-year averages.

Universities and research centers were hit hard. “It was really dire,” indicates Emily Young, who leads medical research grantmaking at the San Diego-based Prebys Foundation. In phone calls with researchers, many told her they had halted ongoing experiments, such as developing measles vaccines for people with autoimmune disorders.

But the thing that really stood out, Young claims, was how the sudden drop in funding was affecting postdocs and early-career researchers. “Young people were going from feeling like they had an avenue for a really promising career … to feeling like they were in a worthless career.”.

So, in May 2025, the foundation awarded $7 million total in emergency grants to seven local institutions, including San Diego State University, the University of California, San Diego and Scripps Research. The grants targeted more than 80 research programs involving early- and mid-career scientists that were facing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost federal funding.

Larger science philanthropies also stepped into the breach. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $55 million total to 30 universities to support 400 postdoctoral researchers. The Alfred P. Sloan and Spencer foundations, among others, partnered to provide 83 quick-turnaround grants of around $25,000 each to researchers whose NSF education grants had been canceled.

Some wealthy universities also offered bridge funding to their researchers; Johns Hopkins University gave awards up to $250,000 to individuals with unexpected funding gaps, and the Yale School of Medicine arranged to fund up to 90 percent of terminated or frozen NIH grants.

In a recent development, after the first bout of funding chaos, science philanthropy Schmidt Sciences announced a more ambitious approach: to develop the science themselves. In January 2026, they revealed intends to construct three ground-based observatories and a space telescope larger than NASA’s Hubble by the end of the decade. The space telescope alone will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and provide open-access data to scientists worldwide, with a special focus on exoplanets and transient events like supernovas.

In November 2026, the philanthropy opened its first round of funding for early-career scientists using the observatory system; individual awards will total up to $2.5 million each.

In a recent development, “Originally, the hope was we would play a more classic philanthropic role,” says Arpita Roy, an astronomer who directs the Astrophysics & Space Center at Schmidt Sciences. But given the federal funding landscape, she says, “it became pretty clear to us, if we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

It has been revealed that while private funding can be a lifeline, Young says, it’s still a temporary measure at best. “We are not going to fill the vacuum of federal funding,” she says. “There is simply not enough philanthropic resource out there to do that.”.

Industry observers note that in 1995, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made a consequential decision: Rather than publish independent recommendations for childhood vaccines, as they had since the 1960s, they would concern one set jointly. Over the next 30 years, a group called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices advised the CDC, with academy input, to expand its recommendations to include chickenpox, hepatitis A and pneumococcal infections. Cases of the three dropped by more than 90 percent, saving thousands of lives.

Recent findings suggest that but in June 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an outspoken vaccine critic, fired all 17 members of ACIP and replaced many with vaccine skeptics. Kennedy also dismissed the academy representatives that informed the group.

Sources indicate that “Essentially, we had no voice anymore,” recalls O’Leary, the pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. He also serves as the AAP’s immunization schedule editor. “So we made a decision to not participate until we could say, ‘OK, this is a body that can be trusted.’ ”.

In July 2025, the academy and other public health groups sued over the ACIP firings. The committee was unable to meet due to the lawsuit, and over the next six months, the CDC removed recommendations from its childhood vaccination schedule including hepatitis A and B, COVID-19 and meningococcal disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics issued its own schedule including those vaccines in January 2026.

Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images Plus.

In a recent development, the loss of trustworthy federal recommendations leaves “an impossible gap to fill,” O’Leary states. But when it came to stepping in, “from my perspective, there was not an alternative.” The academy has since collaborated with the Vaccine Integrity Project, a new group led by Osterholm, to conduct the scientific reviews that inform vaccine recommendations.

Sources indicate that vaccines weren’t the only childhood health matter to get a shakeup. In April 2025, HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children, which formulates newborn screening recommendations for genetic disorders, many of which can be deadly or disabling. Presently, some 98 percent of U.S.-born infants are screened at birth.

Industry observers note that when the genetics community raised concerns, Cynthia Powell, a retired pediatric geneticist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine in Chapel Hill, gathered around 15 representatives of professional medical societies to create the Newborn Screening Collaborative. With support from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, the group began meeting in early 2026.

Industry observers note that while the collaborative cannot give direct recommendations to HHS, it hopes to conduct evidence reviews for states and the small, parent-led advocacy groups that form around rare diseases, Powell indicates. It plans to focus on conditions that already have treatments under development, like a rare metabolic disorder known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Approximate number of NIH and NSF grants canceled or suspended in 2025. Some 5,200 have since been reinstated.

“This Newborn Screening Collaborative is another effort not to leave a complete void,” says Jewel Mullen, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin who was lead editor on a May 2025 newborn screening report for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.

Industry observers note that other researchers are filling gaps in awareness about public health threats. A philanthropy-backed group called the Evidence Collective posted about the diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak before the CDC’s Health Alert Network did. The collective, made up of more than 30 medical communicators, has more than 10 million followers across social media and notched 11 billion impressions in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think that we will ever be able to fully replace the infrastructure that was there through the federal government,” states Madison, a founding member of the collective. But “there is a concerted effort now to look at: How do we take the momentum that we have with these organizations, and then make it sustainable?”.

Although stopgap measures are succeeding so far, scientists see them as Band-Aids at best. “We’re going to do it for as long as we’re needed,” Osterholm claims. But “I look forward to the day when we’re not going to be needed anymore.”.

In April 2025, nearly 400 scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, a recurring, congressionally mandated report, received an email that it was being reevaluated and they were being released from their work. One of them — Rutgers University climate scientist Bob Kopp — wasn’t surprised. “I don’t think you have to speculate very far” to know why, Kopp claims. He cites a directive in the White House’s 2027 budget request to “stop wasting biological and environmental research resources on climate change.”.

However, “there was an immediate and deep sentiment by the science community to continue the work,” indicates environmental engineer Costa Samaras of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who had also been involved with the climate report. He and colleagues asked the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society to help organize the U.S. Climate Collection, a latest set of papers from scientists about climate research, risks and solutions that will keep the public informed until federal assessments resume.

While the work is promising, “a volunteer effort of 170 scientists cannot substitute for a $30 million effort of 600 people,” Kopp claims.

The American Geophysical Union similarly stepped in with crucial financing for the Arctic Report Card, an annual report from NOAA that has provided information about the changing Arctic since 2006. Its editors were blindsided when they found out during a routine meeting in August 2026 that NOAA was withdrawing its support.

AGU’s in-kind offer to support the project just one month later was “tremendous,” says Twila Moon, a glaciologist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, Colo., who edits the report card. “But [it] is not a kind of model that is sustainable into the future.”.

AGU President Brandon Jones agrees. Nevertheless, at the time, the organization “had this sense of what was moral, what was right, what was ethical,” Jones claims. And given AGU’s resources, “it seemed like it was our turn to show up and step up and act like the union that we’ve always been.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Planetary Society, a nonprofit space advocacy organization based in Pasadena, Calif., took the lead on several committees that NASA dropped. In January, the agency cited executive orders as it withdrew financial and logistical support from eight groups of space scientists and experts that advised NASA’s planning teams on exploring asteroids, comets and planets.

“It was pretty well-managed and organized [before], and then really fell apart because of the intrusion of the executive orders,” indicates Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society. The organization now hosts the advisory groups’ websites, documents and meetings. “We’ve basically been having to reinvent this whole system.”.

Chris Gunn, Courtesy of Schmidt Sciences.

Climate.us isn’t the only site saving federal data. In November 2024, many environmental organizations “started preparing for the worst,” says Brittany Janis, executive director of the Open Environmental Data Project. Her group and nine others banded together to create the Public Environmental Data Partners, a network of 400 volunteers that archive environmental data and tools they suspected “would probably be on the chopping block.”.

In February 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency deleted a tool called EJScreen, which maps places where people face high levels of risk from environmental burdens such as hazardous waste and ozone. Within 48 hours, the partnership had stood up EJScreen on a new website, using open-source files to reverse engineer and refine the data pipelines. It has since received 1,000 views a month, Janis says.

Nearly $2 million in philanthropic funding has helped the project pay staff, host data and hire engineers. It has restored the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Future Risk Index, which projects county-level economic losses from climate change; the White House Council on Environmental Quality’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool, which identifies communities overburdened by pollution; and the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data tool, which maps infrastructure at risk of natural disasters.

“We should not misunderstand the administration’s closing off of this data [to mean] that they don’t think data is important,” Janis claims. “They recognize how important it is — and how valuable it is to causes that they disagree with.”.

At the University of Chicago, the Data Mirror Project preserves datasets larger than one terabyte, including those from the U.S. Census Bureau and the National Park Service. The project has a guiding principle: LOCKSS, which stands for lots of copies keeps stuff safe, says colead Lisa Chinn, who is head of research data services at the university library. An agency doesn’t have to delete its data to create problems, she adds. Firing website staff can lead to wonky links, corrupted files and pages that degrade into Wingdings gibberish.

The thought of losing all that data can be stressful, Janis says, but “there’s a lot of parachutes that have gone out.”.

Even as researchers, volunteers and scientific organizations pick up the pieces of the federal science enterprise, some are already imagining newly introduced ways of shaping it. “The world was not perfect in 2024,” notes Rutgers’ Kopp. “Reconstruction is an opportunity to improve upon the way things are done.”.

To Mullen, the epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin, transparency is key. New bodies like the Vaccine Integrity Project and the Newborn Screening Collaborative should make their meetings and deliberations as open as possible, she claims, especially when “people think that those with the loudest voices or the biggest wallets are going to be the ones that have the greatest influence behind the scenes.”.

Powell, of the Newborn Screening Collaborative, is hoping for greater efficiency in the disease recommendation process. Previously, it could take as long as three years to bring a condition from an initial vote to a final recommendation; with the collaborative, she hopes it could take one to three months.

Industry observers note that janis, of the Open Environmental Data Project, hopes to develop more creative and flexible data tools for researchers based on their needs. And Madison from the Evidence Collective and Martin of OnlyMarms believe that the science infrastructure needs to diversify its funding sources to prevent future shocks.

“If we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

It has been revealed that however, Janis notes that there are inherent risks in having the private sector support public goods such as open information. And Kopp warns that “attempts to replace something that was well-functioning … are not going to necessarily end up with something that is better or even as good as what was there before.”.

It has been revealed that at the end of the day, one of the key elements in establishing a new science system is “faith that you will still exist in a year or 10 years or maybe even 20 years,” claims Katharine Jacobs, an environmental scientist who directed a previous National Climate Assessment under President Obama. Without stable institutional funding, “we are all essentially wasting our time, bashing our heads against the wall, trying to create a system that we can’t support,” Jacobs says.

For the Lindsey sisters, being involved in public service — even outside the government aegis — has been empowering, especially during what they see as an otherwise dark period for science.

Industry observers note that they have raised more than $600,000 from individual donations since August 2025. And in February, they received a one-time grant from the Doris Duke Foundation and others that will cover their salaries and benefits until February 2027.

“If we can get the money, I can see us doing this indefinitely,” Rebecca Lindsey says. She still hopes to retire one day, and she fights off worries that the government might come knocking about their unsanctioned work. But “we had a public that trusted us,” she says about jumping into the fray. “It was a risk worth taking.”.
